one_liner: Minimal C QUIC/HTTP3 research stack; beats quiche by ~6-7% on bulk upload and connection setup in one loopback harness.
what_it_does: picoquic is Private Octopus's C implementation of IETF QUIC (RFC 9000/9001/9002/8999, QUIC v2, version negotiation). It also covers DATAGRAM, ACK frequency, the multipath draft and experimental BDP/timestamp drafts, and ships a minimal HTTP/3 (h3zero, static QPACK) with WebTransport. The API centres on a QUIC context (`picoquic_create`) that holds connections and calls back per connection on stream data and events. The caller supplies the clock and does the I/O: it feeds packets in with `picoquic_incoming_packet` and pulls ready (optionally GSO-coalesced) packets out with `picoquic_prepare_next_packet_ex`, either through the bundled socket loop or its own event loop. It is not API-compatible with quiche, so switching means rewriting the integration layer.
how_it_is_fast: The docs describe copy avoidance on both paths. Senders can use a just-in-time API: `picoquic_mark_active_stream` plus the `prepare_to_send` callback, where the app writes straight into the packet being formatted via `picoquic_provide_stream_data_buffer`, so there is no per-stream queue copy. Acknowledged packet structures are recycled through a per-context free list. On receive, a decrypted packet is queued to the stream as-is (no second copy) when the stream frame is its last frame. `picoquic_prepare_next_packet_ex` can return a train of packets for a single UDP GSO `sendmsg`. The benchmarked build used picotls's x86-64 'fusion' AES-GCM engine (loaded only if `ptls_fusion_is_supported_by_cpu()`), and picoquic grows flow-control credit automatically by default because 'flow control tends to limit performance'.
when_to_use: One or two long bulk streams per connection, especially client-to-server upload: 15.8 vs 14.8 Gbps (syscall) and 14.5 vs 13.8 Gbps (io_uring) over quiche on loopback.
Handshake-heavy loads where a small edge matters: 297 vs 277 full handshakes/s on syscall (the io_uring row was inconclusive).

Transport research or experimentation: multipath draft, ACK frequency, BDP and timestamp extensions, and pluggable congestion control (cubic, bbr, bbr1, c4, prague, newreno, fastcc). Virtual time lets you test deterministically on a simulator.
Embedding a small MIT-licensed C QUIC engine into your own event loop, io_uring or DPDK path, since the library never touches sockets or the clock itself.
Non-HTTP protocols over QUIC (for example DNS over QUIC via the companion quicdoq project) or WebTransport and HTTP datagrams via h3zero.
when_not_to_use: Many concurrent streams on one connection: multistream download was 0.55-0.67 Gbps and multistream upload 0.59 Gbps, against quiche's 11-15 Gbps (16-26x slower) in the same run.

RPC-style or lossy workloads: quiche beat it on request/response (0.92x syscall, 0.61x io_uring), small messages (0.67x), close/reset (0.66x), 0-RTT (0.86x) and loss recovery (7.6 vs 11.7 Gbps, 0.65x). Issues #1830 (Cubic stabilization after HyStart) and #1694 (HyStart vs Linux) are still open.
High-rate unreliable DATAGRAM traffic: 72k-91k datagrams/s vs quiche's ~5.1-5.2M. Both rows were inconclusive, but the gap is 57-71x.

Memory-constrained hosts carrying high-BDP flows: the docs warn of hundreds of MB per connection at gigabit rates unless you cap it, and idle footprint was 135 KB vs quiche's 125 KB per connection (syscall).
Production multipath: it tracks an evolving draft, and 2026 fixes for multipath and qlog crashes (NULL derefs #2215 and #2136, qlog double-free #2152, #2188) show that code is still settling.

integration.form: static lib (CMake target picoquic-core, plus optional picoquic-log and picohttp-core; shared libraries via BUILD_SHARED_LIBS since 2026-09-24)
integration.dependencies: picotls (required; -DPICOQUIC_FETCH_PTLS=Y fetches it) and OpenSSL 1.1.1/3.0 by default (the benchmark used 4.0.0). WITH_OPENSSL=OFF falls back to picotls minicrypto, whose AES-GCM the docs call 'very slow'. Threads required. Optional: MbedTLS, libaegis, liburing (WITH_IO_URING).
integration.min_toolchain: C11 with extensions, CMake 3.13+; Visual Studio 2017 solution on Windows
integration.platforms: Linux, Windows, macOS, FreeBSD. CI runs on x86-64 VMs only; ARM32 and Apple M1 rely on user reports. The fusion AES-GCM engine is x86-64 only.
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe. Use one QUIC context (with its connections) per thread and call the API only from that context's network thread, handing work over with picoquic_wake_up_network_thread. A WITH_THREAD_CHECK=ON debug build traps violations.

gotchas: Since commit 8b8c302 (2026-09-17), CMake defaults PTLS_WITH_FUSION=OFF because unimplemented fusion stubs in the vendored picotls crash real connections. The benchmarked build (2b1e14d, May 2026) had fusion on, so a current-master build encrypts through OpenSSL, and nobody has measured whether the upload margin survives that.

Cap memory up front with picoquic_set_cwin_max and picoquic_set_max_data_control. Flow-control credit already granted cannot be withdrawn, and out-of-order data holds whole received packets, so usage can exceed the flow-control limit when frames are small.

A custom loop must call picoquic_prepare_next_packet_ex often enough. In #2190 the maintainer traced stop-and-go throughput to ACK gaps growing to hundreds of ms (keep them under ~25 ms), and the socket-loop docs warn against long work inside callbacks.

Multithreaded servers keep resumption tickets and tokens per thread, and the ticket key is a per-process random value unless set in config. Resume/0-RTT across processes or hosts therefore needs a shared key, and clients only resume from the same thread.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In the same quicperf run, ngtcp2 roughly doubles picoquic's bulk numbers (upload 31.0 vs 15.8 Gbps, download 18.2 vs 8.9-9.7 Gbps) and TQUIC leads on request rate (155k vs 59k rps), so choose those for raw throughput or RPC. Choose picoquic for its research extensions (multipath, BDP/timestamps, many congestion controllers, simulator) in a small MIT-licensed C codebase, or reach for its picoquic-DPDK fork if you can adopt kernel bypass.
verified_claims_summary: The run is victorstewart/quicperf's 2026-06-01 loopback matrix: Linux, harness-owned UDP I/O, CUBIC, one pinned server thread, C++20 -O3 -march=native with LTO. The CPU model was not recorded and the harness tree was dirty. picoquic master 2b1e14d (picotls with fusion, OpenSSL 4.0.0) reached p50 upload of 15.82 vs 14.79 Gbps against quiche 0.29.0 (target-cpu=native, fat LTO) on syscall (1.07x, CI 1.061-1.076; picoquic had 2 client threads, quiche 4), 14.55 vs 13.76 Gbps on io_uring (1.06x), and 297 vs 277 handshakes/s (1.07x). It lost the other 18 of 21 publishable pairwise comparisons.
status_note: Actively maintained under MIT: last push 2026-09-25, first GitHub release v2026.09.24.61fcd56, version string 1.1.53.0. It builds as a normal CMake library, but application docs are thin; the README points to picoquicdemo and the sample folder as the best starting points.
